group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 58-year-old woman who lives independently in a downtown loft and still works part-time as an art-studio registrar presented to the emergency department in mid-afternoon after three days of escalating productive cough, subjective fevers, and right-sided pleuritic discomfort that forced her to sleep bolstered on two pillows; she purposefully withheld her usual morning medications—including sevelamer, calcitriol, and an antihypertensive combination pill—so that the first hospital measurements would reflect her native physiology, and she declined over-the-counter antipyretics or use of the rescue inhaler her primary clinician once prescribed for seasonal wheeze. She was driven by a neighbor and remained conversational throughout the ride, accurately recounting the date, her schedule for an upcoming dialysis planning visit, and details of the artwork currently stored under her care. Past medical background is notable for stage 4 chronic kidney impairment attributed to long-standing hypertensive nephrosclerosis; her nephrologist has discussed pre-emptive fistula placement, but she has not yet required renal replacement therapy. Outpatient laboratories from the last month listed baseline blood urea nitrogen values in the mid-30s and creatinine around 2.6 mg/dL without proteinuria, and she follows strict advice to limit sodium and phosphorus in her diet. She never experienced transient ischemic attack, seizure, or focal neurologic deficit, and there is no reported history of chronic liver disease, connective-tissue disorder, or systemic malignancy. Her immunizations are up to date, including both pneumococcal series and an influenza shot in October. She quit a 12-pack-year cigarette habit fifteen years ago, enjoys a glass of white wine with friends every few weeks, and has never used recreational drugs. On roll-in she sat upright on the stretcher, answering questions in full sentences, oriented to person, place, time, and circumstance, and able to recall three objects at five minutes. Skin was warm, lightly diaphoretic, and capillary refill was brisk; mucous membranes appeared slightly tacky but not frankly dry. Triage nursing staff documented untreated vital signs at sea-level elevation while the patient breathed room air: oral temperature 100.9 °F, regular tachycardic pulse 107 beats per minute confirmed on three-lead telemetry, automated right-arm blood pressure 123/71 mm Hg corroborated manually, respiratory rate 27 breaths per minute with moderate intercostal effort but no supraclavicular retractions, and fingertip pulse oximetry fluctuating between 91 % and 92 % without supplemental oxygen. Neck veins were not distended above the clavicle, and no peripheral edema was noted. Cardiac examination revealed crisp S1 and S2 without extra sounds, murmurs, or rubs. Pulmonary auscultation demonstrated decreased breath sounds and stony dull percussion at the right posterior base with coarse inspiratory crackles just superior to that zone; the left lung transmitted vesicular airflow throughout and percussed resonant. The abdomen was soft and nontender with normal bowel sounds, and there was no flank tenderness. A focused neurologic screen showed equal, reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, fluent speech, normal finger-to-nose testing, and 5/5 strength in all extremities. Capillary glucose obtained prior to venipuncture read 118 mg/dL. Venous blood drawn within ten minutes of bay entry—before any intravenous fluids, antibiotics, or heparinized saline larger than the 2 mL used to lock the catheter—returned a basic metabolic panel of sodium 138 mEq/L, potassium 4.4 mEq/L, chloride 103 mEq/L, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 33 mg/dL, and creatinine 2.8 mg/dL, the latter two consistent with her known renal profile. A complete blood count revealed leukocytosis to 13.6 × 10⁹/L with 86 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 40 %, hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL, and platelets 242 × 10⁹/L. An arterial sample from the right radial artery, drawn while she remained on ambient air, demonstrated pH 7.37, PaCO₂ 36 mm Hg, PaO₂ 76 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 21 mEq/L, consistent with mild hypoxemia and an acid–base state near physiologic neutrality. Serum lactate was 1.6 mmol/L, and high-sensitivity troponin I fell below the analytic threshold. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained fifteen minutes after arrival—before any antimicrobial, diuretic, or ventilatory support—showed a dense right lower-lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a crescentic fluid level that obscured the ipsilateral costophrenic angle, compatible with a reactive pleural collection; heart size and mediastinal contours were within normal limits compared with a film from the prior year. Electrocardiography displayed sinus tachycardia at 108 bpm with nonspecific T-wave flattening but no acute ischemia. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures, a nurse-assisted expectorated sputum sample for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila, and a multiplex respiratory viral PCR panel were dispatched to the laboratory before any empiric therapy. Up to the moment this narrative is filed, the patient has received no intravenous crystalloids, bronchodilators, vasopressors, corticosteroids, antipyretics, or supplemental oxygen beyond minimal saline to keep the arterial catheter patent, ensuring all physiologic observations, laboratory values, and imaging findings above accurately reflect her untreated presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) uses demographics, comorbidities, examination findings, laboratory values, and imaging at presentation.
- Demographics: for a woman, use age minus 10: 58 − 10 = 48. She lives independently, so nursing-home residence adds 0.
- Comorbidities: stage 4 chronic kidney disease adds 10. No malignancy, liver disease, heart failure, or cerebrovascular disease is reported: 0 each.
- Examination: she is oriented; respiratory rate 27 is below 30; systolic BP 123 is at least 90; temperature 38.3 °C is neither below 35 nor at least 40; pulse 107 is below 125. All score 0.
- Tests: BUN 33 mg/dL meets the ≥30 threshold: +20, even though it is near baseline. Arterial pH 7.37 is at least 7.35, sodium 138 is at least 130, glucose 118 is below 250, hematocrit 40% is at least 30%, and room-air PaO₂ 76 is at least 60 with saturation above 90%: 0 each.
- Imaging: right pleural effusion adds 10.
Total: 48 + 10 + 20 + 10 = 88.
Final answer: 88
